name: Diffuse Idiopathic Pulmonary Neuroendocrine Cell Hyperplasia

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: No formal consensus criteria; diagnosis based on histopathology and clinical-radiological correlation

criteria.description: Diffuse proliferation of pulmonary neuroendocrine cells confined to the bronchial and bronchiolar epithelium without invasion
No evidence of invasive carcinoid tumor or other malignancy on biopsy or resection
Presence of characteristic respiratory symptoms and imaging findings such as multiple small pulmonary nodules and mosaic attenuation
Exclusion of secondary causes of neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia such as chronic lung disease or smoking-related changes

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Histopathologic confirmation of diffuse neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia without invasion plus compatible clinical and radiological features
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis often requires multidisciplinary evaluation including pulmonology, pathology, and radiology

searchTerms: worsening shortness of breath with activity

pathognomonic.symptomName: Mosaic attenuation pattern on high-resolution CT
pathognomonic.notes: Radiologic finding highly suggestive of small airway disease
searchTerms: mixed dark and light lung areas

common.symptomName: Air trapping on expiratory CT imaging
searchTerms: air trapped in lungs on exhale
lung air retention seen on CT

common.symptomName: Pulmonary function test showing obstructive or mixed ventilatory defect

occasional.symptomName: Fatigue related to chronic respiratory insufficiency

rare.symptomName: Pulmonary hypertension secondary to chronic hypoxia
searchTerms: lung artery hypertension from low oxygen
pulmonary hypertension due to chronic hypoxia

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests; no specific biomarkers identified
Possible mild hypoxemia on arterial blood gas analysis
imaging: High-resolution CT showing diffuse mosaic attenuation and multiple small pulmonary nodules
Air trapping on expiratory phase CT scans
genetic: No known genetic mutations definitively associated; idiopathic etiology
other: Histopathology demonstrating neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia without invasion
Positive immunohistochemical staining for neuroendocrine markers (chromogranin, synaptophysin)

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of invasive tumor mass on imaging or biopsy
Histopathology showing invasive carcinoid tumor cells
Possible carcinoid syndrome symptoms more frequent
Histopathology showing fibrotic obliteration of bronchioles
Different radiologic pattern with air trapping but no nodules
History of smoking or exposure to noxious agents
Absence of neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia on biopsy

references: Travis WD, et al. WHO Classification of Tumours of the Lung, Pleura, Thymus and Heart. IARC; 2021.
Agarwal R, et al. Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia: clinical features and outcomes. Chest. 2015;148(6):1411-1419.
Orphanet: Diffuse idiopathic pulmonary neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia (ORPHA:617916).
